The sky appears blue because of a phenomenon called Rayleigh scattering. Sunlight, which contains all colors of the visible spectrum, enters Earth's atmosphere and collides with tiny gas molecules like nitrogen and oxygen. These molecules scatter shorter wavelengths of light—blue and violet—far more strongly than longer wavelengths like red and orange, with the scattering intensity increasing as the fourth power of the wavelength's inverse. As a result, blue light is scattered in every direction across the sky, and that scattered blue light is what reaches our eyes when we look up. Violet light is scattered even more, but our eyes are less sensitive to it, and much of it is absorbed higher in the atmosphere, so the sky reads to us as a vivid blue rather than violet. On a clear day, the effect is most pronounced, which is why the sky looks especially blue when the air is clean and dry.

This is also why sunsets appear red and orange: when the sun is low on the horizon, its light travels through a much thicker slice of atmosphere, so most of the blue light has been scattered away before it reaches your eyes, leaving the longer red and orange wavelengths to dominate.
